## Solution

We determine all $f:\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$ satisfying
$$f(2xf(3y))+f\!\left(27y^{3}f(2x)\right)=6xy+54xy^{3}. \tag{P}$$

**Verification of a candidate.** $f(t)=t$ gives $f(2x\cdot 3y)+f(27y^{3}\cdot 2x)=6xy+54xy^{3}$. ✓ So $f=\mathrm{id}$ is a solution. We prove uniqueness.

---

### 1. A cleaner form

In (P), set $t=3y$ (so $y=t/3$, $27y^{3}=t^{3}$) and $u=2x$ (so $x=u/2$). The RHS becomes
$$6\cdot\tfrac{u}{2}\cdot\tfrac{t}{3}+54\cdot\tfrac{u}{2}\cdot\tfrac{t^{3}}{27}=ut+ut^{3}=ut(1+t^{2}).$$
Thus, for all $u,t>0$:
$$\boxed{\,f(uf(t))+f\!\left(t^{3}f(u)\right)=ut(1+t^{2})\,}. \tag{A}$$

---

### 2. Proving $f(1)=1$

Let $c:=f(1)$.

* $(A)$ with $u=t=1$: $f(f(1))+f(f(1))=2$, so $f(c)=1$. $\quad(\mathrm{J})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c,\ t=1$: $f(c\,f(1))+f(f(c))=2c$, i.e. $f(c^{2})+f(1)=2c$ (using $f(c)=1$), hence $f(c^{2})=c$. $\quad(\mathrm{N})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c^{2},\ t=1$: $f(c^{2}f(1))+f(f(c^{2}))=2c^{2}$, i.e. $f(c^{3})+f(c)=2c^{2}$ (using $f(c^{2})=c$, so $f(f(c^{2}))=f(c)=1$), hence $f(c^{3})=2c^{2}-1$. $\quad(\mathrm{O})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c,\ t=c$: $f(c\,f(c))+f(c^{3}f(c))=c^{2}(1+c^{2})$. Since $f(c)=1$, this is $f(c)+f(c^{3})=c^{2}+c^{4}$, i.e.
$$1+(2c^{2}-1)=c^{2}+c^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;2c^{2}=c^{2}+c^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;c^{2}(c^{2}-1)=0.$$
Since $c>0$, we get $\boxed{c=f(1)=1}$.

---

### 3. Two key identities

With $c=1$:

* $(A),\ u=1$: $\;f(f(t))+f(t^{3})=t+t^{3}$. $\quad(\mathrm{B})$
* $(A),\ t=1$: $\;f(u)+f(f(u))=2u$. $\quad(\mathrm{C})$

Subtracting $(\mathrm{C})$ from $(\mathrm{B})$ (with $u=t$):
$$f(t^{3})-f(t)=t^{3}-t. \tag{D}$$

---

### 4. A contraction–dilation argument

Define $\varphi(t):=f(t)-t$; we must show $\varphi\equiv 0$.

* From (D): $\varphi(t^{3})=\varphi(t)$ for all $t>0$. $\quad(\varphi_{1})$
* From (C): $f(f(u))=2u-f(u)=u-\varphi(u)$. But also $f(f(u))=f(u)+\varphi(f(u))=u+\varphi(u)+\varphi(f(u))$. Hence
$$\varphi(f(u))=-2\varphi(u)\quad\text{for all }u>0. \tag{$\varphi_{2}$}$$

Since $f>0$, we have $f(v)=v+\varphi(v)>0$, so $-v<\varphi(v)<v$; in particular $|\varphi(v)|<v$.

**Iterates.** Let $f^{(n)}$ denote the $n$-fold iterate. From $f^{(n+1)}(w)=f^{(n)}(w)+\varphi\!\left(f^{(n)}(w)\right)$ and $(\varphi_{2})$,
$$\varphi\!\left(f^{(n)}(w)\right)=(-2)^{n}\varphi(w),$$
so by summing the geometric series,
$$f^{(n)}(w)=w+\frac{\varphi(w)}{3}\bigl(1-(-2)^{n}\bigr). \tag{$\ast$}$$

(Indeed $f^{(1)}(w)=w+\varphi(w)$, $f^{(2)}(w)=w-\varphi(w)$, matching $(\ast)$; the recurrence is linear in $\varphi(w)$.)

Every iterate lies in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$, so the right side of $(\ast)$ must be $>0$ for **all** $n\ge 0$.

* **Even** $n=2m$: $f^{(2m)}(w)=w+\dfrac{\varphi(w)}{3}(1-4^{m})\to -\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ if $\varphi(w)>0$. Contradiction. Hence $\varphi(w)\le 0$.
* **Odd** $n=2m+1$: $f^{(2m+1)}(w)=w+\dfrac{\varphi(w)}{3}(1+2\cdot 4^{m})\to -\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ if $\varphi(w)<0$. Contradiction. Hence $\varphi(w)\ge 0$.

Therefore $\varphi(w)=0$ for every $w>0$, i.e. $f(w)=w$.

---

### 5. Conclusion

The unique function satisfying the equation is
$$\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\text{for all }x>0.}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE

## Solution

We determine all $f:\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$ satisfying
$$f(2xf(3y))+f\!\left(27y^{3}f(2x)\right)=6xy+54xy^{3}. \tag{P}$$

### 1. A cleaner form

In (P), set $t=3y$ (so $y=t/3$, $27y^{3}=t^{3}$) and $u=2x$ (so $x=u/2$). The RHS becomes
$$6\cdot\tfrac{u}{2}\cdot\tfrac{t}{3}+54\cdot\tfrac{u}{2}\cdot\tfrac{t^{3}}{27}=ut+ut^{3}=ut(1+t^{2}).$$
Thus, for all $u,t>0$:
$$\boxed{\,f(uf(t))+f\!\left(t^{3}f(u)\right)=ut(1+t^{2})\,}. \tag{A}$$

---

### 2. Proving $f(1)=1$

Let $c:=f(1)$.

* $(A)$ with $u=t=1$: $f(f(1))+f(f(1))=2$, so $f(c)=1$. $\quad(\mathrm{J})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c,\ t=1$: $f(c\,f(1))+f(f(c))=2c$, i.e. $f(c^{2})+f(1)=2c$ (using $f(c)=1$), hence $f(c^{2})=c$. $\quad(\mathrm{N})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c^{2},\ t=1$: $f(c^{2}f(1))+f(f(c^{2}))=2c^{2}$, i.e. $f(c^{3})+f(c)=2c^{2}$ (using $f(c^{2})=c$, so $f(f(c^{2}))=f(c)=1$), hence $f(c^{3})=2c^{2}-1$. $\quad(\mathrm{O})$
* $(A)$ with $u=c,\ t=c$: $f(c\,f(c))+f(c^{3}f(c))=c^{2}(1+c^{2})$. Since $f(c)=1$, this is $f(c)+f(c^{3})=c^{2}+c^{4}$, i.e.
$$1+(2c^{2}-1)=c^{2}+c^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;2c^{2}=c^{2}+c^{4}\;\Longrightarrow\;c^{2}(c^{2}-1)=0.$$
Since $c>0$, we get $\boxed{c=f(1)=1}$.

---

### 3. Two key identities

With $c=1$:

* $(A),\ u=1$: $\;f(f(t))+f(t^{3})=t+t^{3}$. $\quad(\mathrm{B})$
* $(A),\ t=1$: $\;f(u)+f(f(u))=2u$. $\quad(\mathrm{C})$

Subtracting $(\mathrm{C})$ from $(\mathrm{B})$ (with $u=t$):
$$f(t^{3})-f(t)=t^{3}-t. \tag{D}$$

---

### 4. A contraction–dilation argument

Define $\varphi(t):=f(t)-t$; we must show $\varphi\equiv 0$.

* From (D): $\varphi(t^{3})=\varphi(t)$ for all $t>0$. $\quad(\varphi_{1})$
* From (C): $f(f(u))=2u-f(u)=u-\varphi(u)$. But also $f(f(u))=f(u)+\varphi(f(u))=u+\varphi(u)+\varphi(f(u))$. Hence
$$\varphi(f(u))=-2\varphi(u)\quad\text{for all }u>0. \tag{$\varphi_{2}$}$$

Since $f>0$, we have $f(v)=v+\varphi(v)>0$, so $-v<\varphi(v)<v$; in particular $|\varphi(v)|<v$.

**Iterates.** Let $f^{(n)}$ denote the $n$-fold iterate. From $f^{(n+1)}(w)=f^{(n)}(w)+\varphi\!\left(f^{(n)}(w)\right)$ and $(\varphi_{2})$,
$$\varphi\!\left(f^{(n)}(w)\right)=(-2)^{n}\varphi(w),$$
so by summing the geometric series,
$$f^{(n)}(w)=w+\frac{\varphi(w)}{3}\bigl(1-(-2)^{n}\bigr). \tag{$\ast$}$$

(Indeed $f^{(1)}(w)=w+\varphi(w)$, $f^{(2)}(w)=w-\varphi(w)$, matching $(\ast)$; the recurrence is linear in $\varphi(w)$.)

Every iterate lies in $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}$, so the right side of $(\ast)$ must be $>0$ for **all** $n\ge 0$.

* **Even** $n=2m$: $f^{(2m)}(w)=w+\dfrac{\varphi(w)}{3}(1-4^{m})\to -\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ if $\varphi(w)>0$. Contradiction. Hence $\varphi(w)\le 0$.
* **Odd** $n=2m+1$: $f^{(2m+1)}(w)=w+\dfrac{\varphi(w)}{3}(1+2\cdot 4^{m})\to -\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ if $\varphi(w)<0$. Contradiction. Hence $\varphi(w)\ge 0$.

Therefore $\varphi(w)=0$ for every $w>0$, i.e. $f(w)=w$.

---

### 5. Conclusion

The unique function satisfying the equation is
$$\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\text{for all }x>0.}$$
